name: Crisaborole (Eucrisa)

lead: Crisaborole (brand name Eucrisa) is a prescription ointment for mild to moderate atopic dermatitis (eczema). It is a nonsteroidal phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4) inhibitor, which means it works on inflammation without being a corticosteroid.

For appearance, the payoff is skin that is less red, scaly and irritated during eczema flares, including on the face and visible areas. In two phase III trials, more patients on crisaborole than on vehicle (the base ointment alone) achieved clear or almost clear skin after 28 days.

paras: It is applied as a thin layer to affected skin twice daily, as directed by a prescriber, and is approved in the US for people three months and older. It is used in flares and can be used alongside regular moisturizing. Improvement is judged over days to weeks.

The most common effect is burning or stinging where it is applied; allergic reactions are rare. It is a prescription medicine, and who should use it is a clinician's decision. Network meta-analyses compare it with corticosteroids and calcineurin inhibitors, which are the standard comparison treatments.

chain: Thin layer applied to eczema patches
Less redness, scaling and itch; skin looks clearer
angle.text: In people with atopic dermatitis, crisaborole is used to bring flares down so the skin looks calmer and clearer. It treats the condition rather than normal skin.

lead: Crisaborole is a nonsteroidal topical phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4) inhibitor in the benzoxaborole family, sold as the 2% ointment Eucrisa in the US and as Staquis elsewhere [1][2]. It was developed by Anacor Pharmaceuticals, originally for psoriasis, and Pfizer later acquired Anacor [2].

The US approved it in December 2016 for mild to moderate atopic dermatitis and later extended use to age three months and above; Canada approved it in June 2018 [2]. In the EU it was authorized but withdrawn from the market between March 2020 and February 2022 at the company's request [2].

For skin appearance, the connection is that treating eczema flares reduces visible redness, scaling and lesions and the itch-scratch cycle. In two identically designed phase III studies, more crisaborole-treated patients achieved a clear or almost clear skin score with at least a 2-grade improvement after 28 days than vehicle-treated patients (32.8% vs 25.4% in one study, 31.4% vs 18.0% in the other) [3].

paras: In the US, crisaborole is indicated for mild to moderate atopic dermatitis in people three months and older [2]. In the EU the authorization covered people two years and older with 40% or less of body surface area affected [2]. A Grokipedia summary notes that it offers a steroid-free alternative to traditional topical therapies [1].

Crisaborole mainly inhibits PDE4B, which appears to reduce the release of inflammatory signaling proteins such as TNF-alpha, IL-12 and IL-23, although Wikipedia notes its specific mechanism in atopic dermatitis is not known [2]. PDE4 inhibition raises intracellular cAMP levels, reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine production [1].
The most common adverse effect is burning or stinging at the application site, and allergic reactions are rare [2].

Two phase III, randomized, double-blind, vehicle-controlled studies (AD-301 and AD-302) enrolled patients aged two years and older with mild or moderate atopic dermatitis who applied crisaborole or vehicle twice daily for 28 days. More crisaborole-treated patients reached clear or almost clear skin with at least a 2-grade improvement (32.8% vs 25.4% in AD-301, p = 0.038; 31.4% vs 18.0% in AD-302, p < 0.001) [3]. A later post hoc analysis looked at crisaborole in treatment-experienced patients [4].

Large network meta-analyses have compared topical treatments for eczema, including a 2023 review of 219 trials with 43,123 patients [5] and a 2024 Cochrane review of 291 trials with 45,846 participants, most industry-funded with a median treatment length of three weeks [6]. A 2023 guideline from allergy and immunology societies draws on these evidence reviews [7].

timeline.event: FDA approves crisaborole ointment 2% for mild to moderate atopic dermatitis. [2]
